entry.title: Opus Kink – “Low Roader”
entry.summary: This summer, Opus Kink released their debut album The Sweet Goodbye. Today, they’ve returned with a new single, “Low Roader,” which is a fucking ripper. The track takes the traditional Scottish folk song “The Bonnie Banks o’ Loch Lomond” — you know, the one that goes “O ye’ll tak’ the high road, and I’ll tak’…
entry.content:
This summer, Opus Kink released their debut album The Sweet Goodbye. Today, they've returned with a new single, "Low Roader," which is a fucking ripper. The track takes the traditional Scottish folk song "The Bonnie Banks o' Loch Lomond" — you know, the one that goes "O ye'll tak' the high road, and I'll tak' the low road" — and folds it into something entirely its own. The original is a gut-wrenching tune about lovers separated by death, but "Low Roader" takes a considerably less solemn approach.

There's a menacing pace to the track, with a bit of swagger creeping into the chorus. The saxophones circle overhead like stalking birds of prey, while surf-rock guitars add another layer of grit. It's an addictive listen that lands somewhere between ska-punk and jazzy rockabilly.

Frontman Angus Rogers shared that:

"Low Roader" is a song concerning complacency, ignorance and historical amnesia. The verse melody is appropriated from the traditional Scottish song "Loch Lomond." The "low road" is the fairy route by which the dead travel back to their home country. It’s already at your door.

Listen below.

entry.title: Oasis Won’t Attend Their Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame Induction
entry.summary: In 2024, Liam Gallagher famously reacted to his first Rock And Roll Hall Of Fame nomination with a tweet that read, “Fuck the Rock n Roll hall of fame its full of BUMBACLARTS LG x.” Oasis did not make it on the list of inductees that year. However, the recently reunited band made it this year.…
entry.content:
In 2024, Liam Gallagher famously reacted to his first Rock And Roll Hall Of Fame nomination with a tweet that read, "Fuck the Rock n Roll hall of fame its full of BUMBACLARTS LG x." Oasis did not make it on the list of inductees that year. However, the recently reunited band made it this year. Liam actually seemed happy about it and insisted he was going to attend the ceremony, though it was hard to tell if he was being sarcastic. Perhaps unsurprisingly, it turns out the Britpop brothers won't be attending.

This year's Hall Of Fame Induction Ceremony is slated for Nov. 14 at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles. It was confirmed by Rolling Stone today that Oasis won't be making an appearance. Earlier this month, it was announced that Noel would be doing his first solo performance since the Oasis reunion at Goldie's EFG Jazz Festival. That's in London, and it's the same night as the ceremony.

The rest of this year's inductees are Iron Maiden, Phil Collins, the Wu-Tang Clan, Sade, Luther Vandross, Billy Idol, and Joy Division/New Order. Phil Collins was looking forward to meeting Oasis since Noel called him the Antichrist in the '90s. Maybe another time.

entry.title: CMA Awards Respond To Backlash Over Red Carpet Exclusions
entry.summary: The 60th annual CMA Awards are happening on Nov. 18 at Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena, and they’re facing backlash after Sammy Kershaw and Rodney Atkins lamented that their request to walk the red carpet was denied. Now, the Country Music Association has issued a statement on the matter. “In recent days, several artists and their fans…
entry.content:
The 60th annual CMA Awards are happening on Nov. 18 at Nashville's Bridgestone Arena, and they're facing backlash after Sammy Kershaw and Rodney Atkins lamented that their request to walk the red carpet was denied. Now, the Country Music Association has issued a statement on the matter.

"In recent days, several artists and their fans have spoken out about this year’s CMA Awards red carpet guidelines," the statement begins. "Like any major televised event, the red carpet has criteria that exists to help manage limited space and the security needs for both the artists and the media. We are deeply sorry anyone felt excluded by those decisions."

"Our organization’s mission is to honor the history and celebrate the excellence of Country Music," it continues. "With this 60th anniversary year, we are working extra hard to simultaneously spotlight the last six decades, while also celebrating what has been a tremendous year in 2026. It’s not easy to do all of that in just one night, but we are up for the challenge."

It concludes, "We also know this is about more than a red carpet, and we are committed to keep listening and keep finding ways to make sure all artists feel welcome and at home here. To that point, we are in touch with Sammy Kershaw’s team and look forward to continuing that conversation."

In Kershaw's initial statement, he wrote:

Well, I just found out some disappointing news and it really hurts me. I have to share my disappointment with the CMA as they have denied my request to walk the red carpet for a few minutes at this year's CMA Awards, and I have to say I'm pretty sad about it.

My wife, Mendy, and I don't get to attend these events very often, due to touring and schedule conflicts. After adjusting my touring schedule, booking our flights and hotels, she was really looking forward to us sharing a special evening together celebrating country music. Then, to find out I was denied the red carpet two weeks before the show, after being strung along for several months and expecting we would be attending, WTF?

After more than 50 years in this business, many millions of records and singles streamed and sold, more than two dozen Billboard charted hits, a CMA Horizon Award nomination, being a lifetime CMA member, that they presented to me in 1992, and being asked to donate my time to play CMA Fest, I would hope I've earned the opportunity to walk the red carpet alongside my wife, as we've done before.

I'm blessed to still be out on tour every year, performing for the greatest fans in the world and doing what I love.

I believe there should be room to recognize the artists who have spent their lives contributing to this organization's success.

I love country music, but never in a million years would I think that a successful country music entertainer (and I'm not the only one) would not be able to walk the red carpet. It's extremely hurtful, embarrassing and very disappointing. I guess the next time I attend the CMA's, it will be in tribute after I'm gone, if I'm lucky.

Then, Atkins chimed in:

I'm incredibly grateful to the fans who've made this career possible. You've always made me feel welcome in country music, and that's what matters most.

I'm having the best touring year of my career. My latest album, True South, made it to the second round of CMA voting for Album of the Year, and my new single, "Years Are Short," could give me charting songs in three different decades.

After more than 20 years as a CMA member and countless CMA Fests I've played for free, Rose and I were denied red-carpet clearance, just like Sammy Kershaw. So we've decided not to attend this year's CMA Awards.

I also believe the artists who helped build the foundation of country music, like Sammy Kershaw, deserve a place in its celebrations.

Country music should never get above its raisin'.

entry.content:
The experimental South Florida duo known as B0YG1RL have a blown-out, chaotic sound that pulls tons of different strains of dance, rap, and hyperpop, running all of them over with a steamroller and them making a beautiful fresco out of the shards. They make party music, more or less, but they do it in intentionally disorienting ways. The duo got a lot of burn when they teamed up with Novagang on the EP EXIT 2B earlier this year. Now, they've got two more tracks.

B0YG1RL recorded the new tracks "i dont recall" and "openinghearts" with Surf Gang producer 4evr, and they've released them together in a double single called new wave*. "i don't recall" sounds like a mutated strain of SoundCloud rap, while "openinghearts" is like a Euro-trance anthem under attack from static white-noise aliens. Cass Morrison shot the "openinghearts" video in New York. Check out both tracks below.

new wave* is out now on Surf Gang/Decent Distribution.

entry.summary: This week, Krill unleashed Secret Language, their first album in over a decade. So far the Boston band has shared “Commemorative Plaque,” “Dominate,” and “Hawaii,” and now they’re back with the title track, which features Fran’s Maria Jacobson on background vocals and Macie Stewart on violin. “‘Secret Language’ is a song about my family, about…
entry.content:
This week, Krill unleashed Secret Language, their first album in over a decade. So far the Boston band has shared "Commemorative Plaque," "Dominate," and "Hawaii," and now they're back with the title track, which features Fran's Maria Jacobson on background vocals and Macie Stewart on violin.

"'Secret Language' is a song about my family, about putting my son to bed," Jonah Furman explains. "The words of the first few verses are Goodnight Moon read backwards, which is something I do with my kids that drives them nuts. But the song is about wanting to know your family members deeply, to know what each other is saying without saying it. And then at the end of the song the kids are asleep and it is me and my wife, and I try to describe how it is to be in love in marriage."

Listen below.

Secret Language is out 11/13 via Exploding In Sound.

entry.title: YouTube Streams Will Once Again Count Toward Billboard Charts
entry.summary: Huge news for chart nerds and aspiring chart-topping musicians: Billboard will soon count YouTube streams again when tabulating its music charts. The change will take place starting in 2027, according to a blog post from YouTube executive and music industry veteran Lyor Cohen. Measuring the popularity of recorded music with charts is a tricky endeavor,…
entry.content:
Huge news for chart nerds and aspiring chart-topping musicians: Billboard will soon count YouTube streams again when tabulating its music charts. The change will take place starting in 2027, according to a blog post from YouTube executive and music industry veteran Lyor Cohen.

Measuring the popularity of recorded music with charts is a tricky endeavor, partially because so many of the vectors are moving targets. What people are listening to is in a constant state of flux, but so is how people are listening. There have always been flaws in Billboard's methodology, like in the '90s, when a song could only crack the primary singles chart, the Hot 100, if it had been officially released as a single, even if it was all over the radio and MTV. Speaking of which, music video plays on TV have never counted toward the charts, even when networks like MTV, VH1, BET, and CMT were dictating cultural taste to a widespread extent.

The internet and television are different beasts, and music videos did factor into Billboard's calculations once they were on YouTube. YouTube's streaming data was first factored into Billboard's tabulations in February 2013, which immediately allowed Baauer's meme-friendly hit "Harlem Shake" to shake up the charts as listeners flocked to hundreds of user-made videos featuring the track. In 2019, Billboard incorporated YouTube's data into its main album chart, the Billboard 200.

But YouTube withdrew its data from Billboard in January of this year, complaining that Billboard's "outdated" system placed too much weight on subscription-backed streams and unfairly deprioritized free, ad-supported streams. "This doesn't reflect how fans engage with music today and ignores the massive engagement from fans who don’t have a subscription," Cohen wrote at the time.

Now, Billboard has relented. "We are returning to the Billboard charts starting in 2027," Cohen writes. "Billboard’s new methodology better reflects how fans engage with music today across both subscription and ad-supported services." Billboard specifies that YouTube stats will inform the rankings beginning with the Jan. 16, 2027 charts, which will measure listening between Jan. 1-7.

The haggling seemed to be over how YouTube streams would be counted on the Billboard 200. Under the current rules, 2,500 ad-supported streams count the same as one full album purchase (physical or digital). The new rules reduce the one album equivalent to 1,500 ad-supported streams. Under both the old and new rules, one album purchase is equal to 1,000 paid/subscription streams. As a result, expect the distinction between the album and singles charts to continue to blur.

entry.title: Paul McCartney & Ringo Starr To Perform With Joe Walsh At VetsAid Benefit
entry.summary: Life’s been good to Eagles member and veteran solo artist Joe Walsh so far. Walsh always headlined VetsAid, a benefit concert that regularly comes to different cities. Next year’s VetsAid is coming to Las Vegas’ MGM Grand Garden Arena Jan. 27, and it’s got a shockingly stacked lineup. Walsh will headline the show, and he’ll…
entry.content:
Life's been good to Eagles member and veteran solo artist Joe Walsh so far. Walsh always headlined VetsAid, a benefit concert that regularly comes to different cities. Next year's VetsAid is coming to Las Vegas' MGM Grand Garden Arena Jan. 27, and it's got a shockingly stacked lineup. Walsh will headline the show, and he'll perform with both of the surviving Beatles.

Joe Walsh announced the VetsAid 2027 lineup on Instagram today, and it's got him performing with "special guests" Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr. Walsh and Starr are brothers-in-law. In 2008, Walsh married Marjorie Bach, whose sister Barbara is married to Starr. They also go back a long way. Walsh co-produced Starr's 1983 solo album Old Wave, and he has played with some of the lineups of Starr's All Starr Band.

But that's not all! The VetsAid lineup also includes Vegas hometown heroes the Killers, who could presumably sell out the MGM Grand seven nights in a row by themselves with zero Beatles on the bill. The show is also set to feature St. Vincent, the War On Drugs, and Lucius, as well as "more surprises." Walsh previously joined the War On Drugs at their own A Drugcember To Remember benefit show last year, and he also played a few songs with them in Philly. The War On Drugs and Lucius both played VetsAid in 2023.

All proceeds from VetsAid go to Nevada veterans and their families. Pre-sale for veterans and active duty servicemen and servicewomen starts 11/10 at 10 a.m. Pacific time, with general on-sale starting 11/13 at 10 a.m.

entry.title: John Summit Asks Fans To Stop Throwing Shit At Him: “It’s Getting Disrespectful”
entry.summary: The plague of fans throwing things at performers continues. Last week, someone in the crowd threw a phone at the Chilean-Mexican star Mon Laferte and hit her in the eye during her Las Vegas show. Now, the big-deal dance DJ John Summit humbly requests that people stop throwing shit at him. John Summit regularly entertains…
entry.content:
The plague of fans throwing things at performers continues. Last week, someone in the crowd threw a phone at the Chilean-Mexican star Mon Laferte and hit her in the eye during her Las Vegas show. Now, the big-deal dance DJ John Summit humbly requests that people stop throwing shit at him.

John Summit regularly entertains vast crowds, and some of the people in those crowds evidently don't know how to act. On Saturday, Summit was in the middle of a show at Fort Worth's Ariat Arena when someone in the crowd threw an unidentified object at him. I can't tell what the thing was from the video. Summit didn't get hurt or anything. He didn't even acknowledge it in the moment. Instead, he just kept shirtlessly posing. (If I looked like that guy, I'd do a lot of shirtless posing onstage, too.)

On his Instagram stories afterward, Summit posted an image of himself looking vaguely stressed out, and he added this text: "can you guys please stop pulling me and shoving phones in my face and throwing shit at me it's getting disrespectful."

Summit apparently has a habit of walking through the crowd mid-show, and this kind of things has happened before.

In the past, Summit has defended Burning Man and gotten into online beefs with Travis Scott, Diplo, and Pete Tong. Regardless of how you feel about any of those situations, he is completely in the right here. Stop throwing shit!

It’s one of those songs where you might not realize that you know it until the gigantic chorus comes in. Crowded House…
entry.content:
The Australian post-punk band Hunters & Collectors released the original version of their song "Throw Your Arms Around Me" in 1984, and the song has lost none of its majestic force since then. It's one of those songs where you might not realize that you know it until the gigantic chorus comes in. Crowded House and Pearl Jam both covered "Throw Your Arms Around Me." A Neil Finn/Eddie Vedder version showed up on a season-two episode of The Bear. Now, there's another "Throw Your Arms Around Me" cover out in the world, this time from the great Australian singer-songwriter Julia Jacklin.

Jacklin just released her excellent album The Gem in September, and she covered Sugar Ray for Triple J during the rollout. In a recent live-in-studio session for SiriusXMU, Jacklin also offered her take on "Throw Your Arms Around Me." Accompanied by a backup singer/guitarist, Jacklin transformed "Throw Your Arms Around Me" from a rousing singalong rocker into a slow, spare, mostly acoustic ballad. The song works beautifully in either context. Below, check out Jacklin's cover and Hunters & Collectors' original video.

The Gem is out now on 4AD. Check out our recent interview with Jacklin here.

entry.content:
Over the years, reigning streetwear brand Supreme has collaborated with culty musicians like Daniel Johnston, Massive Attack, My Bloody Valentine, and Aphex Twin. Now, the company is devoting another collection to Elliott Smith, the widely beloved late singer-songwriter. Smith, who took his own life in 2003, was never known for being especially fashionable. I can't really see the appeal of expressing your affection to Smith through hypebeast clothing, but I've never been Supreme's intended customer base anyway.

On its website, Supreme offers up a short bio of Elliott Smith and announces that it has permission from Smith's estate for a new fall 2026 collection. It drops Nov. 12, and it includes a work jacket, a hoodie, a thermal, a beanie, and three T-shirts, many of them available in different colors. See for yourself whether the clothes are aesthetically appealing enough to get past any instinctive revulsion that you might feel for this kind of thing. You can see some images below and more on Supreme's site.

A few days ago, Hypebeast reported that Supreme are also making NYPD and FDNY merch, so that's the kind of company we're dealing with here.

entry.title: Black Belt Eagle Scout – “Fantasy”
entry.summary: It’s been a little bit since we’ve heard from Black Belt Eagle Scout, aka Swinomish musician Katherine “KP” Paul. She released her last album The Land, The Water, The Sky in 2023. In 2024, she was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, and her new single “Fantasy” is the first song she’s sharing since getting diagnosed. It…
entry.content:
It's been a little bit since we've heard from Black Belt Eagle Scout, aka Swinomish musician Katherine “KP” Paul. She released her last album The Land, The Water, The Sky in 2023. In 2024, she was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, and her new single "Fantasy" is the first song she's sharing since getting diagnosed. It was written after an MS relapse. The song was produced and finished with musicians Claire Glass and Nay Mapalo, who play in a band called Hikes.

"Fantasy" is a lush, sprawling track with lyrics that confront the pressures of outside expectations and a shifting internal dialogue, though the song recognizes that KP has outgrown imposed molds. Except there is one fun part where she sings "Fuck you/ Fuck you ideals/ Fuck what you have to say/ I'm done with you/ I just want to be free/ And listen to the trees." On paper, it seems harsh, but KP sounds reassured. It's a potent reminder that life is so much bigger and beautiful than this modern world acknowledges, and it makes me wanna say fuck all this bullshit, let me please go hang out with trees.

In a press release, KP shared how the song came to be:

I wrote "Fantasy" during a time in my life when I was transitioning out of the nonprofit world and into making music full time. I was feeling really burnt out and disconnected from the work I was doing. Working in the Native nonprofit world, I often felt this pressure to be some kind of superwoman representing Native people, while also trying to fit into systems that didn't always reflect who we are as Native people. I was at a point where I didn't want to keep trying to fit into something that didn't feel right for me anymore. I wanted to make music, feel free, spend time in the trees, and reconnect with myself outside of all those expectations.

Watch the video for "Fantasy" below.

entry.title: Knifeplay – “Toil (Reprise)”
entry.summary: Knifeplay are getting ready to drop an epic on us. In January, Philadelphia slow-crushers, a 2022-vintage Band To Watch, will release What Is Truth?, a new album that apparently lasts for nearly 80 minutes. The sprawling, swooning 10-minute lead single “Love Song” was one of our favorites of the week. Today, we get another taste.…
entry.content:
Knifeplay are getting ready to drop an epic on us. In January, Philadelphia slow-crushers, a 2022-vintage Band To Watch, will release What Is Truth?, a new album that apparently lasts for nearly 80 minutes. The sprawling, swooning 10-minute lead single "Love Song" was one of our favorites of the week. Today, we get another taste.

What Is Truth? opens with a song called "Toil," but that's not the track that Knifeplay have released today. Instead, the band shares "Toil (Reprise)," which comes later in the LP and revisits that opener. The reprise is itself pretty huge, building from gauzy drone-riffs to thundering blackgaze over six minutes.

The track comes with a graphic, disturbing video that frontman Tj Strohmer directed. I watched a few seconds and then let it play in a different tab because I don't really need that in my life. Your mileage may vary. Apparently, it's his homage to Begotten, the silient, experimental 1989 horror film. Some of my friends saw that movie in high school and wouldn't shut up about it for years. Here's what Strohmer says:

This video is a remake or retelling of Elias Merhige’s 1989 silent horror film Begotten, which, in my interpretation, tells the story of the cycle of suffering that has befallen humanity via the metaphorical (or literal?) death of God and subsequent torture and death of "Mother Earth." While I am probably not a Christian, I do not see this story as a blasphemous one; I see it as having empathy for a god, a planet, and a people who, like Mother Earth’s forlorn child, have found themselves helpless, injured, and confused.

Given that the song is primarily instrumental and lyrically simple, it felt like the perfect canvas to tell this story, whose themes are relevant across the whole album. The original film is shocking and uncompromising in its storytelling, which are traits I have always wanted to bring into my own artistry. Despite being an extreme amateur when it comes to video work, with a scarcity of time, resources, and courage, I attempted to tell the story in a slightly milder way that would work for a music video.

Check it out below.

What Is Truth? is out 1/22 on Double Double Whammy.

entry.title: Trapt Make Enemies Out Of Local Openers In Florida
entry.summary: Back in 2020, the onetime nü metal hitmakers Trapt went on an absolutely ridiculous Twitter rampage in defense of Donald Trump’s COVID response. That was the initial impetus, anyway. It turned into a lot of stuff about Trump and also Trapt’s own Pandora numbers, and it led to social media feuds with people like Ice-T…
entry.content:
Back in 2020, the onetime nü metal hitmakers Trapt went on an absolutely ridiculous Twitter rampage in defense of Donald Trump's COVID response. That was the initial impetus, anyway. It turned into a lot of stuff about Trump and also Trapt's own Pandora numbers, and it led to social media feuds with people like Ice-T and the late Power Trip frontman Riley Gale. (Richard Marx also got involved, somehow.) The Twitter spree went viral, and Trapt might be better known today for that now than for their their 2002 song "Headstrong." Trapt are still apparently making enemies, including the local openers from a show that they played over the weekend.

On Friday night, Trapt played their 2002 self-titled album in full at Guadalajara Mexico in Fort Pierce, Florida. They share the bill with the Maine band Sygnal To Noise and the local openers Dirty Crumbums, Fear Of Infirmity, and Limb Breaker. After the show, Dirty Crumbums frontman G Money posted on Instagram that their set was cut to 17 minutes, they were kicked out (for chanting “DCB” during Trapt’s set), and that Trapt or Sygnal To Noise broke Fear Of Infirmity guitarist Tai Vitolo’s amp. (Vitolo was apparently playing with DCB because the punk/groove/ska band split with their guitarist last week.)

Dirty Crumbums' Instagram video shows Chris Taylor Brown asking security to kick out all of the "DCB" chanters. We see them leaving the venue, with one of the band members saying, "They lost half the crowd!... "We didn't see 'Headstrong'!"

In his Stories, Vitolo added, “I think the funniest thing about this whole show is that Signal To Noise paid to play with Trapt. That’s pretty fucking embarrassing, that you paid to be on a fucking bill with a dead band. And if you look it up, it says they’re a one-hit wonder.”

On Sunday, Trapt responded with an Instagram post of a video of their set in Fort Pierce. In the caption, they wrote, "Great show in Fort Pierce the other night, despite a band called 'Dirty Butt Crumbs' going viral courtesy of our great friends at FB for making a post about getting kicked out of the venue for being absolute children. PA issues pushed back the start an hour, so openers had 10 mins cut from their sets and Trapt played at 10 as was scheduled. You should have heard the clapping of the 90% of people in there who were trapt fans. Never seen such crybabies in my life."

entry.content:
Last Thursday, Olivia Rodrigo shared her first-ever Christmas song "take me home (4 christmas)." It has been surprisingly controversial. Holiday songs already tend to be pretty polarizing — some people love 'em, and some people can't stand 'em (moi). But Rodrigo's first go at it is fine, in my opinion.

Over the past few days, however, the internet has gotten into a fuss about how it sounds similar to the Waitresses' 1981 classic "Christmas Wrapping." And although the cheeky vibe is there, it's not a rip-off. Rodrigo even reached out to the band's Christopher Butler months before the song's release. Butler then defended the pop star after plagiarism allegations started to build on the internet. Now, Robbie Williams has entered the conversation after people pointed out similarities to his 2012 song "Candy."

On Saturday, Williams tweeted "Happy Christmas @oliviarodrigo x," which some people interpreted as shade. But this morning, Williams followed up with an Instagram post saying that he didn't mean to go after Rodrigo at all. His post pointed out how we're living in an absurd time where it's easy or trendy to comparison spiral about art. He did, however, jokingly call out Rodrigo for swearing: "Also, I cannot believe how much she swears on stage. And that's coming from me. I'm a Sweary Mary, but she's making me look like a Victorian schoolmistress."

His full message reads:

There's something about the music industry that's been bothering me for a while. People coming after people because they've spotted a similarity between two songs. Some of it I completely understand. Some of it is absolutely justified. Most of it, I think, is complete bollocks. I've had plenty of people come after me over the years because something I've released apparently sounds like something somebody else released. And sometimes I listen and think, fair enough, I can hear that. Other times I think, are you having a fucking laugh?

There are only so many notes. Only so many chords. Only so many ways of putting them together before you inevitably find yourself somewhere somebody else has been. Music has been around for a very long time. We're all going to bump into each other
eventually.

Which brings me to Olivia Rodrigo. I love Olivia Rodrigo. I've loved her since "Brutal." What a fucking record. I wish I'd made it. Also, I cannot believe how much she swears on stage. And that's coming from me. I'm a Sweary Mary, but she's making me look like a Victorian schoolmistress. Anyway. It sounds to me as though she may have accidentally stumbled across a musical echo of mine in one of her new songs. And do you know what? I couldn't care less. I don't know whether there's technically a publishing issue, a copyright issue, or no issue whatsoever. And I don't want to know.

I'm not going after her. Because I think at some point, some fucking sanity has to prevail. Now, I appreciate I'm in a position in my career where I can afford to take that view. Not everybody is. And genuine theft is genuine theft. Artists deserve to be protected. But there's a difference between protecting your work and treating every vaguely familiar sequence of notes as a winning lottery ticket. Some of this stuff has become ambulance chasing. And I think it's disgusting. We all stand on the shoulders of people who came before us. Sometimes consciously. Sometimes without even knowing it. That's how music works. If we keep punishing people for accidentally arriving somewhere somebody else has already been, eventually we're going to frighten the creativity out of everyone.

Anyway. Olivia, if you're reading this, I think you're fucking brilliant. But please stop swearing so much. It makes me feel like I have to keep up. And frankly, I'm already swearing far more than is necessary. Lots of love and Happy Christmas
Rob x

entry.content:
Deftones threw their annual San Diego stadium festival Día De Los Deftones on Saturday at Petco Park. In addition to the headliner/curators, the fest had its usual eclectic mix of acts including Converge, Lip Critic, the Neighbourhood, AFI, Bktherula, Jehnny Beth, Ladrones, and LustSickPuppy. Deftones' own set was properly stacked with hits, and they made time for one tune that hadn't surfaced for 18 years.

The unreleased song "Melanie" is part of Eros, the uncompleted Deftones album that was shelved after a car crash put bassist Chi Cheng in a coma in 2008. Eros, long a Deftones fan holy grail, leaked this summer, a year after frontman Chino Moreno wrote in a fan Q&A that the album would never come out because it would involve "going back to that period and resurrecting unfinished things, and somehow bringing them to completion," when the band would rather focus on new ideas.

However, Deftones are at least willing to nod toward the fan interest in Eros. Deep into their Día De Los Deftones set, they broke out "Melanie" for the first time since 2008. After performing it, Moreno said, "This song doesn't exist." So I guess hearing it is like seeing a ghost? That feels appropriate for the occasion.

Watch the "Melanie" performance below.

entry.title: Sepultura Play Final Show At Massively Downgraded Venue
entry.summary: Sepultura’s farewell show didn’t happen the way that the Brazilian metal titans envisioned it. The band originally planned to play their final show at São Paulo’s Pacaembu Stadium, an important venue for the band. But when the show happened on Saturday night, they had to move it to the same city’s Suhai Music Hall, a…
entry.content:
Sepultura's farewell show didn't happen the way that the Brazilian metal titans envisioned it. The band originally planned to play their final show at São Paulo's Pacaembu Stadium, an important venue for the band. But when the show happened on Saturday night, they had to move it to the same city's Suhai Music Hall, a much smaller venue.

Some context is necessarily here. Sepultura are one of the greatest and most important metal bands in history, and their classics from the '80s and '90s remain influential today. In Brazil, they're national heroes. They're certainly the biggest international rock band ever to come from Brazil. Part of the reason that they wanted to play at Pacaembu Stadium in the first place was the iconic 1991 show where the band played to tens of thousands of Brazilian fans in Praça Charles Miller, just outside the stadium.

As huge as Sepultura were in Brazil, though, the current version of the band is a distant echo of what it once was. Founding frontman Max Cavalera left Sepultura in 1996, and his drummer brother Iggor quit the band in 2006. The Cavalera brothers feuded with each other for many years, but they have since made up, and they play together in the Cavalera Conspiracy now.

American replacement frontman Derrick Green has technically been in Sepultura for longer than Max Cavalera ever was, but he never had a chance to become their definitive leader. (Also, Eloy Casagrande, Sepultura's drummer since 2011, left as part of the great drummer shuffle of 2024, with former Suicidal Tendencies member Greyson Nekrutman replacing him.)

Sepultura announced their global farewell tour in 2023, and they planned for their final show to be a grand sendoff, a celebration of the band's history, but it couldn't really be that without the Cavalera brothers' participation. Earlier this year, guitarist Andreas Kisser, one of only two classic-era Sepultura members, admitted that the Cavalera brothers had turned down an invitation to rejoin the band that they started. As Guitar World reports, Kisser told Metal Hammer, “We did invite the Cavalera brothers. I spoke to Iggor personally on a phone call a few months ago, and we started some communication. Even our managers went to talk to their management and stuff. But they don’t want to be a part of it, and that’s OK. It’s a choice."

Without the Cavalera brothers along, Sepultura's final show simply was not going to be that special of an event. In September, Blabbermouth reported that the gig had been moved from Pacaembu Stadium, which has a capacity of 26,000, to the 9,000-cap Suhai Music Hall. The three announced openers — Brazilian death metalers Krisiun, Phoenix thrash pioneers Sacred Reich, and supergroup Metal Allegiance — still opened the show.

Sepultura's final show wasn't the bast spectacle that the band clearly wanted, but it still looks pretty impressive on camera. As Loudwire reports, the band played a career-spanning 32-song set that featured a bunch of live rarities and appearances from members of bands like Krisiun, Chained Saint, Eminence, Torture Squad, and Ratos de Porão. Jairo Guedz, Sepultura's guitarist in their early years, rejoined the band for a few songs at the end. Even in a smaller room, the classics got thunderous fan reactions. Check out some videos below.

entry.title: The Number Ones: Drake’s “Jimmy Cooks” (Feat. 21 Savage)
entry.summary: In The Number Ones, I’m reviewing every single #1 single in the history of the Billboard Hot 100, starting with the chart’s beginning, in 1958, and working my way up into the present. The column is now biweekly, alternating with The Alternative Number Ones on Mondays. Book Bonus Beat: The Number Ones: Twenty Chart-Topping Hits…
entry.content:
July 2, 2022

  • STAYED AT #1:1 Week

In The Number Ones, I'm reviewing every single #1 single in the history of the Billboard Hot 100, starting with the chart's beginning, in 1958, and working my way up into the present. The column is now biweekly, alternating with The Alternative Number Ones on Mondays. Book Bonus Beat: The Number Ones: Twenty Chart-Topping Hits That Reveal the History of Pop Music.

I remember exactly where I was when Drake tried something. It was June 2022, and I was driving back home after a screamo show. I drove to that show through an absolute fucking squall of a thunderstorm, the type of thing where you find yourself dodging fallen branches on the highway. I probably should've just given up when the weather got bad —pulled over, parked under an overpass, and turned my car right back around when it let up. But no, I had to get to Richmond to see Infant Island, Gillian Carter, Amygdala, and Listless play in the back room of a bike shop. I was glad I went, too. That show fucking ruled.

I live in Charlottesville, and the trip back from Richmond isn't that long, but it feels long, especially when it's late at night and you've got work in the morning. I got into my car right around midnight, and when the clock ticked over to the next day, I hit play on the new album that Drake had just announced a few hours earlier, figuring that I might have to review it the next day. Between the initial drive feeling like a near-death experience and the life-affirming nature of the show itself, I was really primed to like a new Drake album, despite being massively underwhelmed by the few that preceded it. When I hit play and heard a sleek, thumping dance beat come out of my speakers, I got kind of excited. Drake was doing something new! This felt like an event!

Drake had been playing around with club music for years before the sudden release of Honestly, Nevermind, the full-on dance album that was clearly intended to soundtrack all kinds of get-togethers during the post-COVID summer when people were finally gathering in large numbers again. Some of Drake's best tracks had been the ones where he engaged with dance music on one level or another: "Take Care," "Passionfruit," "One Dance." Drake had been in a holding pattern for years before the Honestly, Nevermind moment, going back to the same musical modes and rotely airing his grievances. Maybe, I thought, he'd finally forced himself out of his stasis and taken an artistic left turn. After a song and a half, I realized that this hadn't really happened. He'd just tweaked his formula into something even more boring.

If you'd sat next to me on that drive back to Charlottesville, you probably could've watched my enthusiasm flag in real time. On the one hand, Honestly, Nevermind was a real-deal creative swing, an attempt at a full-album statement that pivoted sharply away from the music that we'd come to expect from Drake and his peers. Drake worked with some of the best collaborators he could find, like the South African amapiano producer Black Coffee and the Maryland-via-Guatemala dance sensation Gordo. With those guys, he knowingly called back to the lush, sleek deep house of past generations, reclaiming that stuff as Black music after so many EDM festivals had robbed the music of its context. His approach to that sound was low-energy greyscale. It was numb and surly and staid and hookless. It got me thinking the man had simply forgotten how to make music that sounds alive.

The funniest thing about Honestly, Nevermind is that another of Drake's A-list pop-megastar peers actually did make the album that he must've thought he was making. Someone else locked in on the glorious history of Black dance music and built a vast, sweeping blockbuster opus to honor it. The album didn't do Thriller numbers or anything, but it was one of the year's most critically acclaimed records, and we'll talk about it in a future column. Drake, meanwhile, thought he was actually doing something by mewling his usual romantic complaints over four-four kickdrums. He adjusted his style musically, but his outlook never changed. Instead, he devoted yet another album to being condescendingly annoyed with the women he's supposedly fucking. It wasn't even remotely compelling anymore. Worse yet, he basically made the whole record without rapping, the one thing that he's really good at doing when he's fully locked in.

So it was pretty funny when the biggest hit on Honestly, Nevermind, to the extent that the album had any big hits at all, was the one where Drake just kept doing what he'd previously been doing. He got together with 21 Savage, one of his many Atlanta buddies, and made a straightforward track where both of them flexed and preened and talked about killing you. The song was the red herring at the end of the album, the one that Drake seemingly threw on just to hedge his bets, and it easily overshadowed all the halfassed experiments that he attempted on the rest of the record. The Drake reset did not work. Instead, the only thing that worked was Drake doing Drake things.

"Jimmy Cooks" came on my car speakers when I was finally reaching the end of my drive back from Richmond, pulling off the highway in a bored and spaced-out haze after nearly an hour of hearing Drake in sleepwalking house-diva mode. With the last song, though, Drake finally got me. People love to hate on Drake, and I am frequently one of those people. But when Drake finds his zone, his music works. On "Jimmy Cooks," he found his zone. It's not a great song or anything, but when we're talking about late-period Drake, it's one of the moments where I think he figured his shit out. He'd tried something, and he'd fucked it all up. When he got back to not trying, he was so much better.

A couple of years after "Jimmy Cooks," another rapper of some repute had some disparaging things to say about Drake's habit of making music with people from Atlanta. This column will get to that whole story eventually, but the claim was always true. Atlanta became the center of the rap universe just before Drake took over as a dominant star, and this particular adversary had an easy time filling a verse with the names of Drake's ATLien collaborators. Drake's Atlanta collaborators mostly don't bring the best out of him, but 21 Savage usually does. At this point, there's a full catalog of Drake/Savage collabs, including but not limited to a full studio album. But "Jimmy Cooks" was only the fourth Drake/Savage track, or the fifth if we're counting the Drake-enhanced version of the Savage song "Issa" that was leaked but never released.

Savage was brand new on the scene when he showed up on Drake's song "Sneakin'" in 2016. Savage broke out of the Atlanta underground when he teamed up with future Number Ones artist Metro Boomin to release the Savage Mode EP in 2016, and he showed up on his first Drake song just a few weeks later. ("Sneakin'" peaked at #28.) That song showed that Drake's bluster got a little more punch when paired with Savage's spooky half-whispered threats. At that point, Savage's rap persona was so luridly, exaggeratedly violent that he didn't really seem like a mainstream star. Soon enough, though, Savage appeared on Post Malone's smash "Rockstar" and racked up more hits, both as a guest and lead artist. It was only a matter of time before Drake and Savage crossed paths again.

In 2020, 21 Savage and Metro Boomin released Savage Mode II, their second collaborative record, and they got Morgan Freeman to host it, giving gravitas-heavy monologues on the nature of snitching like he was DJ Drama. Drake appeared on "Mr. Right Now," which amounted to that album's version of a for-the-ladies track, and he talked about how he dated future Number Ones artist SZA when she was a teenager. The song, which was pretty fun, reached #10. (It's a 6.) A year later, Savage appeared on "Knife Talk," from Drake's otherwise hapless Certified Lover Boy album. The song was built on some eerie pianos and a Project Pat verse taken from an A$AP Rocky record. Drake and Savage had fun on that spooky beat, each doing their own versions of Pat's bloodthirsty flicker-flow, and the track peaked at #4. (It's a 9.)

I wonder if Drake agreed with me that "Knife Talk" was the one Certified Lover Boy song that really worked, since "Jimmy Cooks" definitely felt like Drake's attempt to replicate that magic. Drake, I think, understood that Savage's style is a newer take on the gory, ghoulish Memphis underground rap of the '90s. Drake has family connections in Memphis — it's where his father is from — and that '90s Three 6 Mafia stuff proved to be hugely influential on later rap generations in ways that Drake could grasp. I think that's why Drake and Savage invoked Memphis great Project Pat's voice on "Knife Talk," and I think it's also why "Jimmy Cooks" is built on a sample of fellow Memphis underground legend Playa Fly's 1995 track "Just Awaken Shaken."

"Jimmy Cooks" can't match the swirling, psychedelic menace of a song like "Just Awaken Shaken," and it doesn't even really try. Instead, the Drake track uses the "Just Awaken Shaken" chant as an intro, then switches directly into lush opulence. That lush opulence also comes from a sample — a sped-up slice of "You Were Gone," an obscure 1976 late-career slow jam from Brook Benton, the veteran R&B singer who died in 1988. (Brook Benton's highest-charting single, his 1961 take on the blues traditional "The Boll Weevil Song," peaked at #2. It's a 7.)

Playa Fly got a writing credit on "Jimmy Brooks," as did the four writers of "You Were Gone": Al Goodman and Harry Ray, from the R&B group Ray, Goodman & Brown, along with arranger Sammy Lowe and sideman/guitarist Walter Morris. (Back when they were known as the Moments, Ray, Goodman & Brown reached #3 with 1970's "Love On A Two-Way Street," which later got sampled on Jay-Z's "Empire State Of Mind." It's an 8.) That's a big part of the reason that "Jimmy Cooks" has 12 credited writers. Another reason is that "Jimmy Cooks," like so many Drake tracks, has a ton of producers.

The main "Jimmy Cooks" producer that I feel compelled to mention is the Tay Keith. Drake ushered Tay Keith out of the Memphis underground when they started working together in 2018, and we already covered Tay Keith's rise on the column on Drake and Travis Scott's "Sicko Mode." In the time since I published that column, we have lost Tay Keith. He died of an apparent accidental drug overdose this past June at the way-too-young age of 29. He was one of the great rap producers of his era. I miss him already.

The "Jimmy Cooks" production credits also include CuBeatz, the duo of twin German brothers who also worked on "Sicko Mode," as well as Anderson "Vinylz" Hernandez, a veteran New York producer who works with CuBeatz all the time. Russian-born producer Teslenko Alexandrovich, known professionally as Tizzle, also had something to do with "Jimmy Cooks." Also, the New Jersey club producer Dougie F is credited as a co-writer but not a producer on "Jimmy Cooks." He's got writing credits on a bunch of Drake tracks, and I guess he had something to do with Jack Harlow's "First Class," too. Trying to track down all the songwriting credits for recent columns can make me feel like I'm going crazy with a corkboard and some color-coded string connectors.

Anyway, "Jimmy Cooks." Before he got famous as a rapper, Drake played a character named Jimmy Brooks on Degrassi: The Next Generation. He was a high school basketball star who got paralyzed by a gunshot wound, and Drake spent much of his Degrassi tenure in a wheelchair. When Drake first got famous as a rapper, Jimmy Brooks memes followed him everywhere. So the "Jimmy Cooks" title is Drake riffing on his teen-soap-opera past, acknowledging it even as he talks his shit. It's the same thing that Drake did when he reunited the Degrassi cast in his "I'm Upset" video in 2018. (That's a fun video. Too bad about the song. "I'm Upset" peaked at #7. It's a 5.)

Degrassi doesn't figure into "Jimmy Cooks," though. Instead, the song is mostly Drake discussing his own magnificence. The shooting guard you're dating can only get you seats in the middle row, but Drake can get you courtside. Hoes say Drake's sauve, but he can't get RICO'd. He offers tributes to two rap figures, young Young Thug protege Lil Keed and veteran mixtape DJ Kay Slay, who both died in the months just before "Jimmy Cooks" came out, suggesting that Drake dropped the track almost immediately after recording it.

Drake's most memorable line on "Jimmy Cooks" is also his most toxic: "I can tell her head good before I even know/ Bitch, don't tell me that you model if you ain't been in Vogue." That part was too obnoxious even for Drake. A few months later, on another 21 Savage collab called "Spin Bout U," Drake jokingly retracted that statement: "I know what I said ‘bout bein’ in Vogue/ But just like that R&B group from the ’90s, girl, one call, I’ll get you in Vogue." Clunky wordplay, but at least he realized how shitty the first line was. ("Spin Bout U" peaked at #5. It's a 6.)

I think that Vogue line is fucking stupid in the way that so many Drake lines are fucking stupid. Drake says stupid shit. That's part of the experience. Even though I bump on that line, though, I like the way that Drake locks in on "Jimmy Cooks." Especially after hearing a full album of him halfheartedly singing over house beats, "Jimmy Cooks" finds him playful but self-assured, like he's giving himself an encouraging speech in the mirror. Then 21 Savage shows up, and the track really gets good.

"Jimmy Cooks" came out when 21 Savage was on a run. When Savage first blew up, he had a ton of presence, but he wasn't necessarily a great rapper. That changed. As Savage transformed into a durable mainstream star, he grew sharper and funnier on the mic. He made hits without Drake, too. In 2020, Savage's Metro Boomin collab "Runnin'" reached #9. (It's an 8.) A year later, Savage appeared on J. Cole's "My Life," and that song made it as high as #2. (It's a 7. Cole will eventually appear in this column.) Just a week before "Jimmy Cooks" came out, 21 Savage had a great verse on former Number Ones artist Pharrell's single "Cash In Cash Out." I love that song, and I think Savage's verse is even better than the very strong Tyler, The Creator verse on the same track. ("Cash In Cash Out" peaked at #26. Tyler's highest-charting single, the 2024 Daniel Caesar collab "St. Chroma," peaked at #7. It's an 8.)

On "Jimmy Cooks," 21 Savage gets a superstar entrance. The music drops away, and the aforementioned J. Cole makes a quick cameo, telling you to get the fuck out of his face. Then a different beat comes in, faster and more urgent, and Drake repeats his previous line. (That beat-switch is almost certainly one of the reasons that the song has so many producers.) Drake introduces his guest with a flourish, getting Savage to call you, the listener, a "pussy," stretching out the second syllable and making it sound like even more of a schoolyard taunt. At that point, the way that 21 Savage pronounced the word "pussy" was basically a catchphrase, like the way Too Short says "bitch." Look, that's rap music. If you can find a fun and memorable way to deliver a demeaning cussword, you can write your name in the history books.

21 Savage gets off some great punchlines on "Jimmy Cooks." "Smack the backside of his head like he Bart." "All that workin' out, that n***a must think he a wrestler/ But this ain't UFC, this chopper came with a compressor." "The Glock 4-5 came with a switch/ If I was Will Smith, I woulda slapped him with the stick." That last line is obviously the one that landed the hardest. A couple of months before "Jimmy Cooks" came out, Will Smith, someone who has been in this column a few times, slapped Chris Rock in the face onstage during the Oscars telecast. With that line, Savage advanced the seldom-heard argument that Smith didn't hurt Rock enough — that he should've just gone up on that stage and pistol-whipped him in front of the world. The slap was a crazy moment, but just imagine how much crazier it could've been.

Look, I love this bullshit. I want music to make me feel something, to hit on a visceral level. When 21 Savage says some absurd, over-the-top violent shit, that does the trick for me. It doesn't have to be real. Matter of fact, I prefer it when it's not real. I like it when it's so far outside the realm of realness that it becomes a bleak joke. That's my shit. That kind of good-natured devil-may-care bloodlust used to be pretty common in mainstream rap music, but I don't hear anyone, 21 Savage included, coming up with that kind of face-scrunch line today. Savage's "Jimmy Cooks" verse has at least three face-scrunch moments. That's enough for me to declare it a good song.

"Jimmy Cooks" doesn't even have a proper chorus. There's nothing to get stuck in your head. It's not a moment-defining rap hit, and I can't say that it had the kind of societal impact that a hit song is supposed to have. I honestly don't care, though. "Jimmy Cooks" is two sleek and menacing tracks held together by a dramatic beat-switch moment, and it's two guys talking charismatic and confident shit, floating over those beats. It all works for me. I'm not going to sit here and try to argue that "Jimmy Cooks" deserves classic status, but it's got a lot of the stuff that I want in a big rap hit. This column has recently covered a lot of songs that debuted at #1 and then vanished from the charts. "Jimmy Cooks" is absolutely one of those disappearing hits, and it was gone from the top 10 one month after it came out. Still, I like the song better than most that fit into that category. It feels more like a real song to me.

Anyway, "Jimmy Cooks" wasn't supposed to be a single. Drake really wanted to make the Honestly, Nevermind club-music thing happen. In the 10-minute video for track "Falling Back," Drake staged a wedding with 23 different Instagram models, which was probably supposed to be self-aware comedy but which instead came off as the dumbest kind of megalomaniacal bullshit. In any case, "Falling Back," an extremely forgettable track, debuted at #7 and then vanished. (It's a 4.) Other than "Jimmy Cooks," the only Honestly, Nevermind track where Drake even tried to rap was the relatively energetic "Sticky," which came in at #6. (It's a 6.) None of the other album tracks made it into the top 10. "Jimmy Cooks" is the best song on the album, and it's the only one that people really wanted to hear. I don't think that's a coincidence.

You might've noticed that songs from Honestly, Nevermind did not dominate the Hot 100 in the week after the album came out. Honestly, Nevermind still had enough juice to debut at #1 on the album chart, but it was a relative flop by Drake standards — 204,000 in first-week sales equivalents, or about a third of what Certified Lover Boy did less than a year earlier. Honestly, Nevermind went platinum once, while the "Jimmy Cooks" single is now triple platinum. Both Drake and 21 Savage have tons of songs that are way bigger than that. In October 2022, when the song was already halfway forgotten, Drake and Savage finally made a bare-bones single-shot "Jimmy Cooks" video that only included about half of the song. That music video doubled as an announcement: Drake and 21 Savage had made an entire collaborative album, and it would come out in a few days.

Drake and Savage pushed back the release of their album Her Loss by a week because Drake's immunocompromised friend and producer Noah "40" Shebib got COVID, but the record still came out in the first week of November, and it did a lot better than Honestly, Nevermind. I'd like to think that's because it is a lot better than Honestly, Nevermind. Her Loss got a whole lot more spirit and swagger than basically any other late-period Drake album, admittedly a low bar. It's much more of a Drake record than a Savage one, but Savage's presence still adds edge.

A week after the record's release, eight Her Loss tracks made it into the top 10. But an even bigger superstar had a dominant hit out that week, so none of the Her Loss songs reached #1. Drake seemed annoyed about this. ("Rich Flex," Drake and Savage's highest-charting Her Loss single, peaked at #2. It's an 8. That song is quintuple platinum now, thanks in part to a viral TikTok moment. It's fair to say that "Rich Flex" is a bigger real-deal hit than "Jimmy Cooks," even though only the latter reached #1.)

Drake and 21 Savage have collaborated a bunch of times since Her Loss, but those more recent team-ups don't feel as special. Earlier this year, for instance, Savage chanted the hook on "B's On The Table," a Drake song that reached #15. Savage hasn't been back to #1 since "Jimmy Cooks," but he has put more hits up on the board. Later in 2022, for instance, he appeared on Metro Boomin and the Weeknd's "I Don't Wanna Know" remake "Creepin'," which peaked at #3. (Mario Winans' original "I Don't Wanna Know" peaked at #2 in 2004. That song and "Creepin'" are both 8s.) In 2024, Savage released his American Dream album and made it to #5 with the luxuriously macabre "Redrum." (That's another 8.)

Right now, however, 21 Savage seems to be in a bit of a dry spell. At the very end of last year, he released What Happened To The Streets?, a perfectly solid big-ticket rap record that came and went quietly. Its lead single, the Drake collab "Mr. Recoup," stalled out at #51. Straight-up street-rap isn't big on the charts at the moment, and Savage is nothing if not straight-up street rap. He could always return with another big song, but as of right now, this is the last time we'll see Savage in this column. But Drake will be back. Drake always comes back.

GRADE: 7/10

BONUS BEATS: On Super Bowl weekend in 2018, ICE agents arrested and detained 21 Savage, and he faced possible deportation. Before his arrest, people didn't even know that Savage was born in the UK. He'd been living in Atlanta since the age of seven. Savage couldn't leave the US for years while he fought the charges against him. In 2023, however, Savage finally got his green card. Drake made the announcement on his 2023 song "8AM In Charlotte": "Savage got a green card straight out of the consulate/ Where I go, you go, brother, we Yugoslavian." Here's the video for that song, which peaked at #17:

And here's video of Drake making a surprise appearance with Savage at a Toronto show in 2024, when plenty of Drake's other collaborators were turning on him:

The Number Ones: Twenty Chart-Topping Hits That Reveal The History Of Pop Music is out now via Hachette Books. I'm bookin' up ambition on a kitchen stove. Wait. No, that doesn't work. "Bookin' up ambition" is not a thing. Um. Hmm. "Tommy Books." There we go. It's not great, but it'll have to do. Buy the book so I can throw a party for my day ones.

entry.content:
There's no reason for an Elf sequel. The original movie, which starred Will Ferrell as a human raised by elves who embarks on a journey to meet his birth father, played by James Caan, after discovering he's on Santa's naughty list, has become a classic and holiday must-watch. There's really no need to continue the story. But if U2's the Edge happened to write a sequel, as actor and comedian Andy Richter has revealed. It's such an incredibly random piece of lore that now demands more answers.

On The Daily Beast's Obsessed podcast, Richter, who had a small role in Elf and co-wrote the book Elf Unwrapped: Behind The Scenes Of A Modern Christmas Classic, released last week, told host Matt Wilstein that Canadian film producer Shauna Robertson had been approached about a sequel written by the Edge. Apparently, the musician wanted to discuss the project with her. Richter didn't reveal what the story was about, but said it was reportedly fully written. There's no clear explanation for why it never came to fruition, other than that things simply didn't work out.
